title: The Sabbath: God's day of rest
share: From creation to Hebrews 4: what the Bible says about the Sabbath, when it begins, and how Christians keep it today.
opening_question: God rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy. What is the Sabbath, when does it begin and end, how did Jesus and the apostles keep it, and why do Christians today keep it in different ways? Read every verse, also the ones Christians read in different ways, and let the text speak. Each step asks what the text says and what it means for me.

steps.intro: Background first: God made all things in six days, and each day closed with "the evening and the morning" (Genesis 1:5).
steps.question: What did God do on the seventh day, and what three things does Genesis 2 say He did with it?
steps.apply: Do I treat rest as a gift from God, or as something I have to earn?

facts.text: "rested" is shabath, Strong's: "to repose that is desist from exertion". The word sabbath, shabbath, comes from it: "intermission".
God did not rest because He was tired: He "fainteth not, neither is weary". He rested because the work was "finished".
God "blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it". "sanctified" is qadash; Strong's lists "consecrate", "hallow" and "sanctify". It is the first time the Bible uses this word.
Genesis does not use the word sabbath here, and it records no command to Adam. Readers differ on whether the day was kept from creation or first given to Israel.

steps.question: Before Sinai, what did the LORD give Israel on the sixth day, and what happened when some went out to gather on the seventh day?
steps.apply: Do I trust God enough to stop, even when there seems to be more to gather?

facts.text: This is the first time the Bible uses the word sabbath: "To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the LORD".
Manna kept overnight on other days "bred worms, and stank". The double portion kept for the sabbath "did not stink, neither was there any worm therein".
The LORD asked: "How long refuse ye to keep my commandments and my laws?" This was before the Ten Commandments were given at Sinai.
"the LORD hath given you the sabbath": it is called a gift. Jesus would say "The sabbath was made for man".

steps.question: How do the two tellings of the fourth commandment begin, who must rest, and what reason does each one give?
steps.apply: Who in my home or at my work depends on me to give them rest?

facts.text: Exodus begins "Remember the sabbath day"; Deuteronomy begins "Keep the sabbath day". It is the only one of the Ten Commandments that begins with "Remember".
Exodus gives creation as the reason: "in six days the LORD made heaven and earth". Deuteronomy gives the exodus: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt".
The rest reached everyone: children, servants, cattle and "thy stranger that is within thy gates", "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou".
"rested" in Exodus 20:11 is nuach, Strong's: "to rest that is settle down". "hallowed" is qadash, the same word as "sanctified" in Genesis 2:3.

steps.question: What does God call the sabbath in Exodus 31, between whom, for how long, and what does it show about who sanctifies His people?
steps.apply: What does the shape of my week show about whom I belong to?

facts.text: "sign" is 'owth, Strong's: "a signal", "as a flag". It is "a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever".
The sign is "that ye may know that I am the LORD that doth sanctify you". Ezekiel repeats it: "that they might know that I am the LORD that sanctify them".
"and was refreshed" is naphash, Strong's: "to breathe", "to be breathed upon". God's rest is pictured as taking a breath.
Under the law of Moses the penalty was death: "whosoever doeth any work in the sabbath day, he shall surely be put to death".
It is called "a perpetual covenant". Some read this as binding on all God's people for ever; others read it as the sign of the covenant made with Israel at Sinai.

steps.intro: Background first: in the Bible a day begins at evening. "the evening and the morning were the first day" (Genesis 1:5).
steps.question: When does a Bible day begin and end? What did Nehemiah do "when the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the sabbath", and when did the women rest and come to the sepulchre?
steps.apply: How could I prepare before a day of rest begins, so that it is truly rest?

facts.text: The Day of Atonement, a yearly sabbath, was kept "from even unto even". "even" is ereb, Strong's: "dusk". Jews have kept the weekly sabbath the same way, from sunset to sunset.
Nehemiah shut the gates as dusk came "before the sabbath" and kept them shut "till after the sabbath".
In Capernaum Jesus taught "on the sabbath day". The sick were brought to Him "at even, when the sun did set": the sabbath was over.
"that day was the preparation, and the sabbath drew on". "preparation" is paraskeue, Strong's: "readiness". The women "rested the sabbath day according to the commandment".
They came "when the sabbath was past", early on "the first day of the week". In Matthew 28:1 "week" is sabbaton, the word for sabbath; Strong's: "the interval between two Sabbaths".
So the seventh day is the day before the first day of the week, the day the women found the tomb. On today's calendar that is Saturday, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset.

steps.question: What does Isaiah call the sabbath, what does God promise the stranger and the eunuch who keep it, and what did Jeremiah and Nehemiah warn against?
steps.apply: Is my day of rest a burden I carry, or a delight I look forward to?

facts.text: "call the sabbath a delight": "delight" is oneg, Strong's: "luxury".
Isaiah ties the day to the heart: "not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words". The promise: "Then shalt thou delight thyself in the LORD".
Isaiah 56 opens the sabbath to outsiders: "the sons of the stranger" who keep it, "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people". Jesus quoted this in the temple.
Jeremiah: "bear no burden on the sabbath day". Nehemiah found men "treading winepresses on the sabbath" and selling fish and ware in Jerusalem.

steps.question: Why did the Pharisees object in the corn fields, what example did Jesus give from David, and what two things did He say about the sabbath and the Son of man?
steps.apply: Do I use God's commands to serve people, or to judge them?

facts.text: Picking grain by hand in a neighbour's field was allowed: "thou mayest pluck the ears with thine hand". The Pharisees objected to doing it on the sabbath.
"The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath". Some read this as Jesus restoring the sabbath to its first purpose; others as Jesus loosening it.
"the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath". Matthew adds "in this place is one greater than the temple" and quotes Hosea: "mercy, and not sacrifice".
"the priests in the temple profane the sabbath, and are blameless": the temple offerings went on "every sabbath".

steps.question: What did Jesus ask before He healed the withered hand, what did He say to the ruler of the synagogue, and how did He answer when they said He had broken the sabbath?
steps.apply: Who near me is still bound, and how can my day of rest be a day of doing good?

facts.text: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?" Matthew: "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days".
The ruler said "There are six days in which men ought to work". Jesus answered that each of them would "loose his ox" on the sabbath; how much more should she "be loosed from this bond".
"loose" and "loosed" are the same Greek word, luo, Strong's: to "loosen". The ox is loosed for water; the woman is loosed from Satan's bond.

John records the charge "he not only had broken the sabbath" and the answer "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work". Readers differ on whether John reports what Jesus did or what His accusers claimed.

steps.question: What was Jesus' custom on the sabbath day at Nazareth, and what did He tell His disciples to pray about their flight?
steps.apply: What are my habits of worship, and would anyone call them my custom?

facts.text: "as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day". In Capernaum He "taught them on the sabbath days".
"custom" is etho, Strong's: "to be used (by habit or conventionality)". Luke uses the same word for Paul in Acts 17:2, "as his manner was".

Of the days of trouble to come, Jesus said: "pray ye that your flight be not in the winter, neither on the sabbath day". Some read this as His followers still keeping the sabbath; others as the hardship of fleeing when gates were shut and travel was limited.

steps.question: Where did Paul go on the sabbath, what did the Gentiles ask at Antioch, and where did Paul find people praying at Philippi?
steps.apply: Where are people gathering to hear the word of God, and how can I be there?

facts.text: At Antioch the Gentiles asked to hear these words "the next sabbath", and "came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God".
At Philippi they went "by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made", and spoke to the women there.
In Corinth "he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks".
Some see in this Paul's own practice of keeping the sabbath; others see him going where the Jews already met, to show them "that this Jesus, whom I preach unto you, is Christ".

steps.question: On which day did Jesus rise and appear to His disciples? What happened "upon the first day of the week" at Troas and at Corinth, and on what day was John "in the Spirit"?
steps.apply: How does the resurrection shape my week?

facts.text: Jesus "was risen early the first day of the week". He came to the disciples that evening, and again "after eight days".

At Troas the disciples "came together to break bread" on the first day, and Paul spoke "until midnight". Counting days from sunset, that evening was Saturday night; counting from midnight, Sunday night. Readers differ on which.
At Corinth each was to "lay by him in store" on the first day, "that there be no gatherings when I come". Some read this as a church offering on a meeting day; others as setting money aside at home.

"on the Lord’s day": kuriakos, Strong's: "belonging to the Lord". Many read it as Sunday, the day of the resurrection; others as the sabbath, of which the Son of man is "Lord"; others as the prophetic day of the Lord.
The New Testament never calls the first day of the week the sabbath, and no verse moves the sabbath to it. Churches that gather on Sunday ground it in the resurrection.

steps.intro: How Christians keep it today: three main views. Each brings its own verses; read them all and let the text speak.
steps.question: What does Paul say about judging one another over "the sabbath days", what is "a shadow of things to come", and how should believers who see the days differently treat each other?
steps.apply: Do I hold my convictions about the day with love for believers who see it differently?

facts.text: "shadow" is skia, Strong's: "shade" or "a shadow". Paul goes on: "but the body is of Christ".

The seventh-day view (Seventh-day Adventists, Seventh Day Baptists, many Messianic believers): the day was blessed at creation, written in the Ten Commandments, kept by Jesus, the women and Paul, and all flesh will worship "from one sabbath to another". They read Colossians 2:16 of the yearly feast days, and point to those who "keep the commandments of God".

The Lord's Day view (Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches): Christ rose on the first day and met His disciples on it, the church gathered on it "to break bread", and Revelation names "the Lord’s day". Some of these churches call Sunday the Christian Sabbath; others keep it as a day of worship without the Sabbath laws.

The rest in Christ view (many believers across churches): the sabbath was "a shadow of things to come", fulfilled in Christ, who gives rest, so no day is required: "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind". The council at Jerusalem did not name the sabbath among the things asked of Gentiles; others answer that it did not name stealing or lying either.

Galatians 4: "Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years", turning again to "weak and beggarly elements". Some read this of the Jewish calendar; others of the pagan calendar the Galatians came from, since Paul says "how turn ye again".

Outside history, not Scripture: Ignatius (about AD 110) and Justin Martyr (about AD 150) wrote that Christians met on the first day. In AD 321 the emperor Constantine made Sunday a day of rest by Roman law. For centuries some churches kept both days.

steps.intro: Closing: whatever day we keep, Scripture points past the day to the rest God gives.
steps.question: What rest does Hebrews say still remains for the people of God, how do we enter it, and what does Jesus promise all that labour and are heavy laden?
steps.apply: Have I entered God's rest, or am I still trying to earn what He gives?

facts.text: "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God". Here "rest" is sabbatismos, Strong's: a "sabbatism"; the BSB says "a Sabbath rest". In the rest of the chapter the word is katapausis, "reposing down".
Hebrews joins three rests: God's rest on "the seventh day", Israel's rest in the land under Joshua ("Jesus" in verse 8 is Joshua), and a rest still open: "To day if ye will hear his voice".
Readers differ: some see in Hebrews 4:9 a sabbath-keeping that remains for believers; others see the weekly sabbath fulfilled when we have "ceased from his own works" in Christ; many hold both.
"I will give you rest" is anapauo, Strong's: "to repose", "to refresh". The very next chapter opens "on the sabbath day".
